title: Easy Healthy Matcha Cake (4 Ingredients, Sugar Free)
description: Healthy 4 ingredient matcha soufflé fruit cake made with no added sugar. This gluten free, flourless matcha cake is soft, mini and perfect for small batch baking.

hero.alt: A hand holding a square slice of easy healthy matcha cake close up showing the golden-green sponge with bright green matcha icing drizzled on top against a white tile background

thumbnail.alt: A hand holding a square slice of easy healthy matcha cake with bright green matcha icing drizzled on top and more cake slices on parchment paper behind

instructions.text: Add the fruit (apple and banana) and matcha to a high-powered food processor or blender. Blend until smooth.
Add in the almond butter and egg. Blend again until fully combined.
Transfer the batter to a small lined baking tin.
Allow to cool fully (or chill in the fridge). Slice and enjoy!

notes: Use overripe bananas for maximum natural sweetness.
Let it cool fully or chill before slicing for the best structure.
Add white chocolate chips if you want a sweeter twist.
Store in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 3 days. Can also be frozen and thawed prior to eating.

story.subtitle: 4 Ingredients, Sugar Free
paragraphs: this 4 ingredient matcha cake is one of those recipes you look at and almost side eye, lol. from the ingredient list, it's made of mainly just fruit and egg, so i understand the suspicion. is it really a cake? well, yes and no! it's nowhere near your traditional cake in texture or taste, it's best described as a cross between a soufflé and an underbaked cake, but there's really no other way to name it, lol. i know this intro might not be the most convincing sell, and that's not my intention, because it really is delicious, has no added sugar, and the texture is so creamy!

i just want to be upfront from the start that this isn't your traditional cake, but it is a delicious and healthy sweet treat, especially if you're a matcha lover. the texture sits somewhere between a soufflé and a soft pudding cake, delicate and light without being hollow. that softness comes from blending everything together properly rather than any whipping or folding, the egg and almond butter bind it while the fruit keeps it moist. it's sweetened entirely by the apple and banana, so the sweetness is gentle rather than a sugar hit.

use the ripest banana you have, the kind with plenty of brown spots. it gives you a lighter structure and does a lot of the sweetening on its own. you can also use two bananas instead of the apple and banana combo for an even sweeter, softer result, or two apples if you want something lighter and less sweet.

this cake is quite matcha forward, so the quality of what you use actually shows. culinary grade is affordable and works fine day to day, but ceremonial grade gives a more vibrant colour and a sweeter, less bitter flavour. start at 1 tablespoon if you want it subtle, 1.5 if you want it bolder, and taste the batter before you commit either way. the caffeine and l-theanine combo in matcha also gives you a steadier lift than a coffee or sugar crash would.

the almond butter might look like an odd thing to put in a cake, but it's what holds the batter together alongside the egg, and it adds a subtle nuttiness that works well against the earthy matcha. it also means the natural sugars from the fruit digest more slowly, so you're less likely to crash an hour later.

i actually prefer this cold, straight from the fridge. it firms up a little and the matcha flavour tastes more developed. the first time i made it i cut a slice while it was still warm because i couldn't wait, and it fell apart everywhere, so now i make myself wait until it's fully cooled or chilled.

this is a small batch recipe, so you just need a blender and a small tin, something around 15 by 10cm works well. if your tin is a lot bigger the batter spreads too thin and bakes faster, so keep an eye on it. double the ingredients and size up the tin if you're feeding more than one or two people.

if you want to dress it up, a simple matcha icing does the job, just a powdered sweetener, a teaspoon of matcha and enough water or milk to make it drizzle. or fold a handful of white chocolate chips into the batter before baking if you want something sweeter.
if you're into matcha desserts, i'd also point you to my no bake matcha ganache bars and matcha marshmallows.

faq.question: How do I store this mini matcha soufflé cake?
faq.answer: Store in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 3 days. The texture actually improves after a few hours of chilling as it firms up and the matcha flavour deepens. It can also be frozen for up to 1 month. Thaw in the fridge overnight or at room temperature for about 30 minutes before eating.

faq.question: Can I use only banana or only apple?
faq.answer: Yes, you can absolutely use 2 bananas or 2 apples instead of one of each. Using 2 bananas gives a sweeter, softer result with a more pronounced banana flavour. Using 2 apples creates a slightly lighter, less sweet cake. Both work well, so go with whichever matches your taste preference and what you have on hand.

faq.question: Is this healthy matcha cake gluten free?
faq.answer: Yes, this recipe is naturally gluten free because it contains no flour of any kind. The structure comes entirely from the blended fruit, almond butter, and egg. It's also paleo-friendly and dairy free, making it suitable for quite a few dietary needs at once.

faq.question: What type of matcha works best in baking?
faq.answer: Culinary grade matcha works perfectly in baked recipes and is the most affordable option for everyday baking. I personally prefer using organic ceremonial grade matcha when possible, as it has a more vibrant green colour and a sweeter, less bitter flavour. Either will work well in this recipe, so use whatever you have.

faq.question: What size baking tin should I use?
faq.answer: A small baking tin works best for this recipe since it's a small batch. I use something roughly around 15cm x 10cm (6 x 4 inches) or similar. You can also use a small square tin. If your tin is too large, the batter will spread too thin and bake faster, so keep an eye on it. If it's too small, it may need a few extra minutes in the oven.

faq.question: Can I make this matcha cake without almond butter?
faq.answer: Yes, you can swap the almond butter for another nut butter such as cashew butter, which is a little more neutral in flavour. If you need a nut-free version, sunflower seed butter is a good substitute. Tahini could also work but will add a slightly bitter, sesame flavour that may compete with the matcha.

faq.question: Can I add a frosting or topping to this matcha cake?
faq.answer: Absolutely. A simple matcha icing made with powdered sweetener (such as powdered monkfruit), a teaspoon of matcha, and a splash of water or milk mixed to a drizzleable consistency looks beautiful and adds a little extra sweetness. White chocolate chips stirred through the batter or melted on top also work really nicely.

tips: Use an overripe banana with lots of brown spots for the best natural sweetness and a lighter structure in the baked cake.
Let the cake cool fully or chill in the fridge before slicing. It's quite soft and delicate when warm, and slices much more cleanly once set.
Adjust the matcha quantity to suit your taste. 1 tbsp gives a subtle green tea flavour, 1.5 tbsp gives a bolder, more vibrant result.
For a sweeter version, fold a handful of white chocolate chips or dark chocolate chips into the batter before baking.

alternatives: Ceremonial or culinary grade both work
Increase or decrease quantity to taste
